slide.title: Describe It, Don't Copy
slide.body: Five small tiles labelled Medium, Texture, Era, Colour, Mood, with arrows into one generated flat vector image of a runner in orange, teal and white. Small tag: AI Image Generation · Lesson 5.

scenes.voiceover: Many people get a strong look by adding the words in the style of, and the name of a famous living artist. It seems quick. But it borrows someone else's life's work without asking. There is a better way, and it gives you more control.

slide.title: Describing a Style Without Copying Artists
slide.body: AI Image Generation and Visual Design · Lesson 5 of 12. Five empty tiles: Medium, Texture, Era, Colour, Mood.

scenes.voiceover: A style is the set of visual qualities that make images look like they belong together. And you can describe almost any style with five attributes.

slide.title: 1 Medium · 2 Texture and line
slide.body: Medium: gouache painting · linocut print · 3D clay render · 35mm film photograph · flat vector illustration. Texture and line: rough paper grain · clean thin outlines · visible brush strokes · smooth gradients. Small generated swatch beside each.

scenes.voiceover: The first is the medium. What does the image seem to be made with? A gouache painting, a linocut print, a clay render, a film photograph, or a flat vector illustration. The second is texture and line, the surface and the edges. For example, rough paper grain, clean thin outlines or visible brush strokes.

slide.title: 3 Era · 4 Colour · 5 Mood
slide.body: Era or influence: 1970s travel poster · mid-century modern · early digital pixel art (a period, not a person). Colour: limited palette of coral, teal and off-white, slightly faded. Mood: energetic and playful · calm and quiet · bold and confident.

scenes.voiceover: The third is era or influence. This is a period or a general tradition, not a person, like a nineteen seventies travel poster, or mid-century modern. The fourth is colour, the palette and its strength. And the fifth is mood, the feeling, such as calm and quiet, or bold and confident.

scenes.on_screen_text: Five attributes plus composition and lighting
scenes.voiceover: Add the composition and lighting words from lesson four, and you have a complete style description that you can use again and again.

slide.title: Why not name living artists?
slide.body: 1. Style is linked to an artist's income and reputation, and many have not agreed · 2. The legal position is unclear and differs between countries: a risk for you or your client · 3. Some tools block or change prompts with artists' names

scenes.voiceover: So why not name living artists? First, an artist's style is linked to their income and reputation, and many artists have not agreed to have their work imitated by AI. Second, the legal position is unclear and differs between countries, so it can create risk for your business or your client. Third, some tools block or change prompts that include artists' names.

slide.title: Ingredients, not a chef's name
slide.body: Left, ticked: 'slow-cooked beans with smoked meat, garlic and orange' with a simple illustrated bowl. Right, crossed out: 'Cook it like Chef X' with an empty chef silhouette. No real chef named.

scenes.voiceover: Here is a way to think about it. Describing a style by its attributes is like describing a dish by its ingredients and flavours. Slow-cooked beans with smoked meat, garlic and orange tells a cook what to make. Cook it like a famous chef only works if you copy that chef, and it teaches you nothing about the dish.

scenes.stock_query: runner on beach path at sunrise
scenes.voiceover: Let's meet Renata. She runs a small sportswear brand in Recife, Brazil. She wants her campaign images to feel active, warm and local.

slide.title: Renata's style description
slide.body:
Style: flat vector illustration with bold geometric shapes (medium),
clean edges and a light paper grain (texture),
inspired by 1980s sports posters (era),
limited palette of sunset orange, deep teal and white (colour),
energetic and optimistic (mood)

scenes.voiceover: Instead of naming an artist, she writes a five-attribute style description. You can read it on screen. It asks for a flat vector illustration with bold geometric shapes, clean edges and a light paper grain, inspired by nineteen eighties sports posters, in sunset orange, deep teal and white, with an energetic and optimistic mood.

slide.title: Two subjects, one style
slide.body:
A runner on a beach path at sunrise, low angle, empty space at the top.
[Style description]

A pair of running shoes on a boardwalk, close-up, seen from the side.
[Style description]

scenes.voiceover: She tests it on two different subjects. The first prompt is a runner on a beach path at sunrise, from a low angle, with empty space at the top. The second is a pair of running shoes on a boardwalk, in close-up, seen from the side. She adds the same style description to each one.

slide.title: A shared look
slide.body: Two generated images side by side: illustrated runner on a beach path (no real person) and plain running shoes on a boardwalk (no brand marks). Labels under both: same palette · same shapes · same poster feel.

scenes.voiceover: Both images share the orange, teal and white palette, the bold shapes and the poster feeling, even though one shows a person and the other shows a product. Renata now has a style that belongs to her brand, and she can explain every part of it to her team.

slide.title: One word fixes it
slide.body: Before: shoe image with almost no grain, label 'a light paper grain'. After: shoe image with clear grain, label 'a clearly visible paper grain'.

scenes.voiceover: But she notices one problem. In the shoe image, the paper grain is almost invisible. So she changes a light paper grain to a clearly visible paper grain, and generates again. Now the two images match more closely.

scenes.on_screen_text: One movement word is not enough
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to swap an artist's name for one art movement word, like pop art, and stop there. That still leaves the model to guess the medium, colour and mood. And never use a real brand's name, logo or a film or game character to get a look.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Five attributes: medium, texture, era, colour, mood. 2. No living artists' names: attributes give more control. 3. Test the style on different subjects.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, describe a style with five attributes: medium, texture, era, colour and mood. Second, do not name living artists in prompts. It raises ethical and legal questions, and attributes give you more control. Third, test your style description on different subjects to check that it creates a consistent look.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below, you will write a five-attribute style description for a fictional sportswear brand from Brazil, and test it on two different subjects. It takes about twenty minutes. In the next lesson, we learn about keeping images consistent. See you there.
